documents.title: Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
tiers: Minor Uses Permitted for AI Tools
AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted
Specific Expectations and Notes for AI Use
documents.summary: OSU's official guidance for instructors on AI in teaching and learning. Part I sets rules for instructor use (approved tools, no student work in unapproved tools, review and disclosure of AI-made materials and AI-assisted feedback, human grading); Part II is a syllabus statement template with five icon-coded options from 'Do Not Use' to 'AI Use Encouraged'; Part III advises how to write a detailed course statement and revisit it each term.

units.anchor: integrating generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching and learning offers tremendous possibilities
units.policy: Integrating generative AI into teaching and learning offers tremendous possibilities.

units.anchor: integration must reflect our shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity
units.policy: AI integration in teaching and learning must reflect OSU's shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence.

units.anchor: This guidance supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom in designing engaged learning experiences
units.policy: The guidance supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom in designing engaged learning experiences that may include the use of AI.

units.anchor: protecting the privacy and security of individual and institutional data
units.policy: The guidance aims to maintain transparency, uphold educators' ethical responsibilities, and protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data.

units.anchor: enable machines to perform complex tasks beyond the reach of traditional programming
units.policy: AI refers to a broad set of advanced digital technologies, rooted in statistics, computer science, and cognitive psychology, that enable machines to perform complex tasks beyond the reach of traditional programming.

units.anchor: represents a subset of software tools that use questions, prompts, and other inputs
units.policy: Generative AI is a subset of software tools that use questions, prompts, and other inputs to generate human-like output such as a written document, software code, or a product design.

units.anchor: standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings that are embedded in other software
units.policy: GenAI includes both standalone offerings such as ChatGPT and offerings embedded in other software such as Microsoft 365's Copilot.

units.anchor: You are welcome to use AI tools.
units.policy: Instructors and staff are welcome to use AI tools.

units.anchor: instructors and staff are encouraged to utilize
units.policy: Instructors and staff are encouraged to use OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools whenever possible.

units.anchor: OSU employees may explore other AI tools, provided no confidential, sensitive, or student information
units.policy: OSU employees may explore other AI tools provided no confidential, sensitive, or student information (e.g., personally identifiable information, student or employee records, research data) is included.

units.anchor: University Information and Technology (UIT) is the authority on and maintains the list
units.policy: University Information and Technology (UIT) is the authority on, and maintains, the list of OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools.

units.anchor: Using OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools ensures:
units.policy: Using OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools ensures integrated security measures, standardized protocols, enhanced data privacy, access to technical support, and institutional protections.

units.anchor: may not input student work into any AI tools or applications that are not approved
units.policy: To protect student privacy, meet legal obligations, and uphold enterprise security, instructors may not input student work into any AI tools or applications that are not approved by OSU.

units.anchor: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy
units.policy: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use of artificial intelligence.

units.anchor: Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.
strongly encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement if AI or AI tools
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement whether AI will be used to substantially create, augment, or refine instructional materials, or to provide initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials with a rubric.

units.anchor: may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments.
units.policy: Instructors may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments.

units.anchor: instructors are strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage
units.policy: If an instructor uses AI in a substantial way to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, the instructor is strongly encouraged to disclose that AI usage in a syllabus statement.

units.anchor: Instructors are required to review instructional materials created by AI to ensure the highest quality
units.policy: Instructors are required to review instructional materials created by AI to ensure the highest quality, accuracy, and appropriateness.

units.anchor: may direct students to use AI applications and tools as part of their learning
units.policy: Instructors may direct students to use AI applications and tools as part of their learning in the course.

units.anchor: AI tools that are not on the OSU Recommended and Approved list may be required
units.policy: Instructors may require AI tools that are not on the OSU Recommended and Approved list, as long as the assigned activities do not require students to enter their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information.

units.anchor: must use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools if the student is required to enter
units.policy: Instructors must use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools if students are required to enter their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into the AI tool.

units.anchor: When possible, instructors are encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools
units.policy: When possible, instructors are encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools as part of the requirements for course activities and assignments.

units.anchor: initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric
units.policy: Instructors may use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.

units.anchor: instructors are ultimately responsible for assigning grades based on their human evaluation of student work
strongly encouraged to disclose to students in their syllabus statement if they will use
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to disclose to students in their syllabus statement if they will use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools to provide initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials with a rubric.

units.anchor: only OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools may be used to provide such review
units.policy: Only OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools may be used to provide initial review, feedback, or scoring of student work.

units.anchor: may not input student work to any AI tools or applications that are not recommended
units.policy: Due to privacy and data security concerns, instructors may not input student work to any AI tools or applications that are not recommended and approved by OSU.

units.anchor: required to review feedback for students created by AI to ensure the highest quality, accuracy
units.policy: Instructors are required to review AI-created feedback for students to ensure the highest quality, accuracy, and appropriateness for the course and the student.

units.anchor: should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines
units.policy: AI tools may be relevant to student learning but should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines.

units.anchor: When AI use is permitted, care must be taken to use these tools responsibly.
students are responsible for reviewing individual course policies and understanding appropriate use in each course
units.policy: Instructors differ in their approach to AI, and students are responsible for reviewing individual course policies and understanding appropriate use in each course.

units.anchor: Please contact the instructor if you have questions about specific AI tools
units.policy: Students should contact the instructor if they have questions about specific AI tools and the allowable usage of AI tools in the course.

units.anchor: Choose one of the options below to copy/paste here
units.frag_end: to tailor this part of your statement
units.policy: Instructors choose one of the icon-coded syllabus options (Do Not Use; Minor Uses Permitted; AI Tools Integrated by Assignment; AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted; Specific Expectations and Notes) and tailor it to the course.

units.anchor: to generate or edit any portion of the substance of your work is not permitted
units.frag_start: The use of any AI tools
units.policy: Under the Do Not Use option, using any AI tools (including ChatGPT, Copilot, or Claude) to generate or edit any portion of the substance of student work is not permitted unless explicitly noted in the assignment instructions.

units.anchor: you are not allowed to use AI for your coursework beyond these limited non-substantive supports
units.policy: Under the Do Not Use option, students may not use AI for coursework beyond limited non-substantive supports embedded in everyday tools such as grammar check, slide design suggestions, and search engines.

units.policy: Under the Minor Uses Permitted option, students must be the sole author of all work.

units.anchor: You may use AI in some minor ways.
units.policy: Under the Minor Uses Permitted option, students may use AI in some minor ways that the instructor lists as acceptable, and may not use AI for uses the instructor lists as not allowed.

units.anchor: Always review individual assignments for specific instructions.
attribute that use by putting that language in quotation marks and adding a citation
units.policy: (Optional template clause) Students who use language generated by an AI tool must attribute that use by putting the language in quotation marks and adding a citation.

units.anchor: students are permitted to integrate AI into some of the substantive work of the course
units.policy: Under the AI Tools Integrated by Assignment option, students may integrate AI into some substantive work of the course, with permissible uses determined by individual assignments.

units.policy: Unless otherwise noted, students should be able to demonstrate how they contributed to the work they submit for an assignment.

units.anchor: required to keep drafts of assignments and generative AI logs that demonstrate how you used
units.policy: As an example requirement, instructors may require students to keep drafts and generative AI logs that demonstrate how they used AI and what portion of an assignment's content was generated by AI.

units.anchor: In this course, you are encouraged to experiment with AI and AI tools.
You should not enter creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into AI tools.
if one of the above icons does not suit your policy
units.policy: If none of the icon options suits the course policy, instructors may use the Specific Expectations and Notes option and add specific expectations and detailed instructions for student use of generative AI.

units.anchor: both the visual indicator and a detailed description of the specific application
units.policy: Instructors should use both the visual icon and a detailed description of how the policy applies, in the syllabus and in assignment-specific language.

Students encounter different policies across their courses and need specific detail to help them understand
units.frag_end: approach to AI in the course.

units.anchor: detailed, transparent statements also help to hold students accountable in student conduct proceedings
units.policy: Clear, detailed, transparent statements help to hold students accountable in student conduct proceedings.

units.anchor: Examples of specific tasks for which students may be allowed to use AI
units.frag_start: Examples of specific tasks for which students may be allowed
units.policy: Instructors should include examples of tasks for which students may be allowed to use AI, such as generating ideas, polishing or editing drafted text, outlining an essay, designing slides, reviewing content, self-quizzing, or other studying.

units.anchor: Examples of specific tasks for which students may not be allowed to use AI:

units.policy: Instructors should include examples of tasks for which students may not be allowed to use AI, such as any use during a quiz or test, generating content used directly in an assignment (code, text, images), solving assignment problems, writing a first draft, writing a discussion post, or analyzing data.

units.anchor: AI tools that you do or do not want students to use
units.policy: Instructors should name AI tools that they do or do not want students to use, if specific examples should be called out.

units.anchor: Briefly, why you have selected policy (e.g., to support skill development
units.policy: Instructors should briefly explain why they selected the policy (e.g., to support skill development or because the discipline takes a specific stance on AI).

units.anchor: Revisit the statement each term.
units.policy: Instructors should revisit and review their AI statement each term, before each quarter begins, and add information as needed.

units.policy: Instructors should use OSU resources: CTL and Ecampus offer additional guidance and example language for syllabus statements.

documents.title: Generative AI Guidelines for Ecampus Course Development
documents.summary: Ecampus guidelines for faculty and Ecampus staff using generative AI while developing online courses. Ecampus encourages AI that advances innovation and streamlines development, but asks for careful consideration of uses that affect authorship, instructor presence or student interaction (instructor voice simulation, chatbots, AI grading), approved tools only, full faculty review, clear labeling of AI-made learning objects, and a syllabus acknowledgment of substantial AI use.

units.anchor: Faculty have the same broad freedom, as they do when developing courses in other modalities
units.policy: Faculty developing Ecampus courses have the same broad freedom as in other modalities to select and develop content customized to the course.

units.anchor: Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development
units.policy: Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development, while upholding the authenticity and quality of the student learning experience.

units.anchor: Ecampus will adhere to OSU’s Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
units.policy: When faculty or Ecampus staff use generative AI in course development, Ecampus will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning and the Ecampus-specific guidelines.

units.anchor: significantly affects authorship, instructor presence, or student interaction in the course
units.policy: Ecampus staff and faculty partners should carefully consider any generative AI use, routine or experimental, that significantly affects authorship, instructor presence, or student interaction in the course.

units.anchor: creating new learning content that is not originally authored by the faculty
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include creating new learning content that is not originally authored by the faculty.

units.anchor: generating or simulating the instructor’s voice, image, or persona in learning content
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include generating or simulating the instructor's voice, image, or persona in learning content.

units.anchor: creating course chat bots
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include creating course chatbots.

units.anchor: using tools that promote AI-assisted grading
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include tools that promote AI-assisted grading (e.g., auto-grading in Perusall or Gradescope), due to potential impact on teaching quality and regular-and-substantive interaction requirements.

units.anchor: using generative AI in ways that substantially shape the course’s content, instructional approach, or delivery
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include using generative AI in ways that substantially shape the course's content, instructional approach, or delivery.

units.anchor: Ecampus staff will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer
units.policy: Ecampus staff will discuss the implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer for the desired use case.
units.policy_type: NEW:Provide faculty AI development and support

units.anchor: we will consider issues and risks that are outlined in the AI Decision Tree
units.policy: For all uses, Ecampus will consider the issues and risks outlined in the AI Decision Tree to guide the decision to use AI.

units.anchor: Any use of voice automation should follow the three recommendations
units.policy: Any use of voice automation should follow the three recommendations in the Ecampus Voice Automation and AI document.

units.anchor: applying professional judgement on a case-by-case basis when deciding to use voice automation
units.policy: Decisions to use voice automation should apply professional judgement on a case-by-case basis.

units.anchor: being transparent when it’s employed
units.policy: Use of voice automation should be transparent when it is employed.

units.anchor: Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full
units.policy: At this time, Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full.

units.anchor: Ecampus staff will use only OSU’s approved Gen AI tools when working with faculty-created
units.policy: Ecampus staff will use only OSU's approved GenAI tools when working with faculty-created instructional materials for course development.

units.anchor: Use of non-OSU approved AI tools requires instructor permission.
will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy
units.policy: Any AI-generated content used in a course requires full review by the faculty developer, who is accountable for its accuracy.

units.anchor: Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly.
the label should appear within the media itself
units.policy: When AI-created learning objects are used in video or media that could be used outside the course, the label should appear within the media itself.

units.policy: Courses that use AI to create, augment, or refine content in a substantial way will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum.

documents.unit: College of Engineering (Academic Integrity Resources for Faculty)
documents.title: AI Chatbot Policy Example
documents.summary: An example course AI-chatbot policy offered by the College of Engineering to faculty. It allows chatbots as a library-like resource for fixing errors, understanding code, verifying self-developed algorithms, small code snippets and elements of reports, forbids having AI write software or documents, warns that submitted generated work is an integrity violation, and grounds the rules in critical thinking, licensing risk and industry career expectations.

units.anchor: ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI, or similar AI chatbots as you would a library resource
units.policy: Students are allowed to use ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI, or similar AI chatbots as they would a library resource.

units.anchor: use ChatGPT to find solutions for errors the same way you would use Stackoverflow
units.policy: Students may use ChatGPT to find solutions for errors the same way they would use Stack Overflow or other Internet resources.

units.anchor: to understand and improve software you are developing
units.policy: Students may use AI chatbots to understand and improve software they are developing.

units.anchor: You ARE allowed to use AI chatbots to verify algorithms.
You will learn more if you develop your algorithms yourself
units.policy: Students will learn more if they develop algorithms themselves and use a chatbot to verify them, rather than taking the shortcut of asking ChatGPT to generate the algorithms.

units.anchor: the critical thinking skills that AI cannot replace
units.policy: Developing algorithms oneself teaches more about the problem and the critical thinking skills that AI cannot replace.

units.anchor: there are guaranteed to be problems for which AI cannot propose algorithms or solutions
you will be unable to deliver the value your employer expects from a practicing engineer
units.policy: Students who have not developed the critical thinking skills to develop solution algorithms on their own will be unable to deliver the value employers expect from a practicing engineer.

units.anchor: allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code
units.policy: Students are allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code, as they would online references like Reddit or language-specific websites.

units.anchor: do not introduce software license restrictions or the possibility of copyright, trademark, trade secret
units.policy: In industry, small code snippets from any source must not introduce software license restrictions or copyright, trademark, trade secret, or confidentiality violations that could put the company in legal peril.

units.anchor: be cautiously selective about the number and size of code snippets you include
units.policy: Students should be cautiously selective about the number and size of code snippets they include, whether from programming websites or an AI chatbot.

units.anchor: wiser and safer to adapt the principles demonstrated in those snippets to your own code
units.policy: It is wiser and safer to adapt the principles demonstrated in snippets to one's own code and context rather than pasting something into the code verbatim.

units.anchor: Practicing this kind of appropriate use as a student will help establish a foundation
units.policy: Practicing appropriate use as a student helps establish career behaviors consistent with an employer's code of ethics.

units.anchor: allowed to use chatbots in manners similar to the above for generating written reports
units.frag_start: You ARE allowed to use chatbots
units.policy: Students may use chatbots in manners similar to the above for generating elements of written reports or other creative elements, but not whole blocks or reports.

units.anchor: the same possibilities of not learning to think, write, or be creative on your own
units.policy: Using chatbots for written or creative elements carries the risk of not learning to think, write, or be creative on one's own, and being less able to meet employer expectations.

units.anchor: never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking and good judgment
units.policy: Students should never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking and good judgment to assess the correctness and validity of the results.

units.anchor: You won't get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output
units.policy: Students will not get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output from AI or any other source.

units.anchor: abdicating your creative thought processes to any tool won't necessarily grow your abilities
units.policy: Abdicating creative thought processes to any tool will not necessarily grow one's ability to think creatively.

units.anchor: thoughtful and judicious about how much you use these or any tools as a replacement
units.policy: Students should be thoughtful and judicious about how much they use these tools as a replacement for their work rather than as a supplement to it.

units.anchor: send me an email explaining your planned use
units.policy: Students who are unsure whether an intended use of an AI chatbot is allowed should email the instructor explaining the planned use, and the instructor will give feedback on whether it is allowable.

units.anchor: NOT allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you
units.policy: Students are not allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write their software or their documents for them.

units.anchor: we instructors have tools to identify code and documents that were generated
units.policy: Instructors have tools to identify code and documents that were generated by AI.

units.anchor: Any student that submits generated responses will be subject to an Academic Integrity violation.
prepare you for a career in industry, where you will be expected to solve problems
units.policy: OSU aims to prepare students for an industry career in which they will be expected to solve problems through critical thinking and adhere to industry norms for integrity and ethical behavior.

units.anchor: You will not be expected to let a tool do all your work for you
units.policy: In industry, students will not be expected to let a tool do all their work without understanding the engineering problem-solving process.

units.anchor: being able to assess if its results are credible and reliable enough to be trusted
units.policy: Engineers must be able to assess whether a tool's results are credible and reliable enough to be trusted for business-critical decisions.

units.anchor: that's good preparation for being in industry with a broad toolkit at your disposal
units.policy: Using AI chatbots for the allowed purposes to understand their capabilities and limitations is good preparation for industry.

units.anchor: you will limit your career opportunities to those that do not require
units.policy: Using AI chatbots to do one's work to skate by with minimal thought and effort will limit career opportunities.

units.anchor: will continue to increase in the fields of software engineering and computer science
units.policy: The use of AI and machine learning tools will continue to increase in software engineering and computer science.

units.anchor: they were not designed to be learning tools, or to understand the context or nuances
units.policy: AI chatbots were not designed to be learning tools or to understand the context or nuances of a particular software problem.

units.anchor: learn and develop a strong foundation in the fundamental principles and concepts of software development

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
documents.title: Guidance on Drafting AI Use Policies
documents.summary: EECS's June 2026 school-wide statement setting a common floor for AI use across EECS courses while instructors set course rules. It covers faculty use (review and disclosure, approved tools for grading), student use (a restrictive fallback when the syllabus is silent, IDE assistants count as GenAI, point-of-submission disclosure, explain-and-defend), research use (advisor/committee norms, venue rules, verification, research disclosure tiers), syllabus requirements, and academic integrity (no grade sanctions in syllabi, detectors not sole evidence, MOSS/JPlag and behavioral evidence). Appendix A defines nine categories of AI use for coursework.

units.anchor: AI tools have become a part of how work is being done: in industry
units.policy: AI tools have become part of how work is done in industry, in research, and increasingly in the classroom.

units.anchor: This statement establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses
units.policy: The statement establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses so as to set clear expectations.

units.anchor: individual faculty will set course-specific rules, this document provides the common floor and vocabulary
units.policy: Individual faculty set course-specific rules, while this document provides the common floor and vocabulary.

units.anchor: developed using the OSU College of Science Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (September 2025)
units.policy: The statement was adapted for EECS from the OSU College of Science Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (September 2025) and aligns with CTL guidance and the AI@OregonState guidelines.

units.anchor: Where those documents conflict with this one, OSU policy governs.
this document will be updated to align with it when finalized
units.policy: A College of Engineering AI policy is in development, and this document will be updated to align with it when finalized.

units.anchor: Initial version. Developed by Anita Sarma, Associate Head, EECS
units.policy: The policy has a version history; the initial version (June 2026) was developed by the EECS Associate Head.

units.anchor: is the category of AI this policy addresses.
units.policy: The policy addresses Generative AI: systems built on foundation models (LLMs, vision-language models, small language models) that generate human-like output such as text, code, images, audio, or other media.

units.anchor: GenAI systems include standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows
units.policy: GenAI systems covered by the policy include standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows that incorporate these models.

units.anchor: it means GenAI unless otherwise specified
units.policy: Where the document refers to 'AI', it means GenAI unless otherwise specified.

units.anchor: Faculty may use GenAI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments.
Faculty are required to review instructional materials created by GenAI to ensure the highest quality
units.policy: Faculty are required to review instructional materials created by GenAI to ensure the highest quality, accuracy, and appropriateness.

units.anchor: they are strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage
units.policy: Faculty who use AI in a substantial way to create, augment, or refine instructional materials are strongly encouraged to disclose that AI usage in a syllabus statement.

units.anchor: Routine grammar assistance, search features, or autocomplete do not require disclosure.
tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials
units.policy: Faculty may use OSU Recommended and Approved GenAI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.

units.anchor: Grades must reflect the faculty member's own evaluation of student work.
must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used in any part
units.policy: Faculty must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used in any part of the grading or feedback process.

units.anchor: Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work
units.policy: Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work, because they carry the data privacy and institutional protections required for student records.

units.anchor: Faculty must explain their GenAI use policy in their course.
Students may not recognize that AI-assisted features in common development tools constitute GenAI use
units.policy: Students may not recognize that AI-assisted features in common development tools constitute GenAI use under the policy.

units.anchor: Students may use AI tools when course policies explicitly permit it.
When no policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed
units.policy: When no course policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed.

units.anchor: any other AI use must be arranged with the instructor of record before using it
units.policy: When no course policy is stated, any AI use other than routine grammar corrections must be arranged with the instructor of record before using it on coursework.

units.anchor: Search features and autocomplete do not require arrangement or disclosure.
students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit
units.policy: Regardless of what AI use is permitted, students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit.

units.anchor: exists on a spectrum from light assistance at one end to full content generation
units.frag_start: AI use exists on a spectrum
units.policy: AI use exists on a spectrum from light assistance to full content generation, with the full taxonomy of use categories in Appendix A.

units.anchor: Course policies will specify which categories apply to each assignment.
AI embedded in tools you already use counts as GenAI use under this policy.
GitHub Copilot, VS Code or Cursor assistants, and similar IDE features fall within this policy
units.policy: GitHub Copilot, VS Code or Cursor assistants, and similar IDE features fall within the policy even when they feel more like autocomplete.

units.anchor: applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones
units.policy: When a course restricts or requires disclosure of GenAI use, the restriction or disclosure applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones.

units.anchor: When you use AI on permitted work, disclose it at the point of submission
units.policy: Students who use AI on permitted work must disclose it at the point of submission.

units.anchor: identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work
units.policy: The disclosure must identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work it contributed to.

units.anchor: For agentic tools, describe the task given and the extent of its autonomy.
A one-line disclosure is sufficient in most cases.
For guidance on citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats
units.policy: For citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats, students are referred to the OSU Library's GenAI guidance.

units.anchor: engagement may carry its own AI use restrictions beyond what the syllabus states
units.policy: Work with an external sponsor or industry partner may carry its own AI use restrictions beyond what the syllabus states.

units.anchor: Check with your instructor before using AI tools on sponsor-related deliverables.
Recording the instructor or other students is permitted only when the instructor allows it
units.policy: Recording the instructor or other students is permitted only when the instructor allows it or as a documented disability accommodation.

units.anchor: upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an AI tool
units.policy: Students must not upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an AI tool without the instructor's permission.

units.anchor: This section applies to research work by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty
units.policy: The research section applies to research work by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty, including theses, dissertations, manuscripts, grant proposals, technical reports, and documents submitted to examination committees.

units.anchor: Where venue, sponsor, IRB, or funder rules are stricter, those rules govern.
Treat venue rules as the primary constraint and this policy as the floor.
units.policy: Because venues set their own fast-changing AI rules, researchers should treat venue rules as the primary constraint and this policy as the floor.

units.anchor: The major advisor sets AI use norms for research conducted under their supervision.
AI use expectations should be set with the full committee and documented early
units.policy: For thesis and dissertation work, AI use expectations should be set with the full committee and documented early, such as at the program of study meeting or sooner.

units.anchor: AI tools may be used for grammar checking, search, and autocomplete without prior approval
units.policy: Where no research AI norms have been set, AI tools may be used for grammar checking, search, and autocomplete without prior approval.

units.anchor: any substantive use requires prior approval.
units.policy: Where no research AI norms have been set, any substantive AI use requires prior approval.

units.anchor: The final product must be the researcher's, reviewed and revised to that standard.
Blindly using or following AI output is itself an integrity concern.
The researcher is the author and accountable for the work.
AI fabricates citations, misstates prior work, produces plausible but incorrect analyses
units.policy: AI fabricates citations, misstates prior work, produces plausible but incorrect analyses, and can reproduce text from existing sources without attribution.

units.anchor: Every factual claim, citation, quantitative result, and code path must be independently verified
units.policy: Every factual claim, citation, quantitative result, and code path in research must be independently verified.

units.anchor: AI-assisted text should be checked for similarity to existing work
units.policy: AI-assisted research text should be checked for similarity to existing work.

units.anchor: The intellectual content (research question, design choices, analysis decisions, interpretation) must be the researcher's own.
Treat AI as a tool; authorship belongs to the researcher.
Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code
units.policy: Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code to an advisor, committee, or reviewer.

units.anchor: most major venues now require disclosure of substantive AI use, and some prohibit specific uses
units.policy: Researchers should follow venue rules first; ACM, IEEE, NeurIPS, NIH, NSF, and most major venues require disclosure of substantive AI use and some prohibit specific uses.

units.anchor: disclose substantive use in methods, acknowledgments, or an authorcontribution statement
units.policy: Where venue rules are silent, researchers must disclose substantive AI use in methods, acknowledgments, or an author-contribution statement.

units.anchor: tool, task type, and scope.
units.policy: Research AI disclosures must state the tool, task type, and scope.

units.anchor: Disclose any image-editing or imagegeneration process specifically.
The same expectation applies to documents submitted to examination committees.
Do not upload sensitive or confidential material to nonapproved AI tools.
other people's unpublished work, such as a coauthor's draft or a collaborator's code
units.policy: Material that must not be uploaded to non-approved AI tools includes proprietary or sponsor-restricted material, identifiable human-subjects information, and others' unpublished work (a coauthor's draft or collaborator's code) used without permission.

units.anchor: Sponsor agreements and IRB protocols may restrict AI use further.
cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own
units.policy: Prior work published under a copyright transfer (IEEE, ACM, Elsevier, Springer) cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own.

units.anchor: Rewrite, paraphrase with citation, or obtain permission.
units.policy: AI assistance does not change self-plagiarism rules; researchers must rewrite, paraphrase with citation, or obtain permission.

units.anchor: recommended that students run a similarity check to other existing works, using
units.policy: Students are recommended to run a similarity check (e.g., Draft Coach) on all documents submitted to examination committees.

units.anchor: Students should escalate disagreements to the Associate Head of Graduate Programs (AHGP).
The school of EECS expects every course syllabus to include an AI statement.
reflects OSU’s strong encouragement and anticipated future requirement
units.policy: The EECS syllabus expectation reflects OSU's strong encouragement and anticipated future requirement.

units.anchor: with tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted use
units.policy: CTL provides a GenAI syllabus statement template with tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted use.

units.anchor: what students are and are not permitted to do with AI across this course
units.policy: The syllabus statement should cover the student AI use policy: what students are and are not permitted to do with AI across the course.

units.anchor: permissions should align with course learning objectives so that grades reflect actual student mastery
units.policy: AI use permissions should align with course learning objectives so that grades reflect actual student mastery of those objectives.

units.anchor: Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill
units.policy: Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill, and the AI policy for that assessment must reflect that expectation.

units.anchor: Assignments that deviate from the course default, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly
units.policy: Assignments that deviate from the course default AI policy, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly in the assignment prompt.

units.anchor: Assignments that follow the course default need no additional statement.
Syllabi must not specify grade sanctions for academic misconduct
units.policy: Syllabi must not specify grade sanctions for academic misconduct.

units.anchor: sanction determinations belong to the College Hearing Officer
units.policy: Sanction determinations for academic misconduct belong to the College Hearing Officer.

units.anchor: Faculty who need support drafting syllabus statements or designing AI-resilient assignments can request a consultation
units.policy: Faculty who need support drafting syllabus statements or designing AI-resilient assignments can request a consultation with CTL.
units.policy_type: NEW:Provide faculty AI development and support

units.anchor: Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and / or falsification under
units.policy: Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and/or falsification under OSU's Code of Student Conduct.

units.anchor: presenting AI-generated content as your own work without disclosure.
units.policy: Plagiarism includes presenting AI-generated content as one's own work without disclosure.

units.anchor: Where AIgenerated text or code is incorporated into a submission, it must be attributed
units.policy: Where AI-generated text or code is incorporated into a submission, it must be attributed in the work itself.

units.anchor: Submission-level disclosure does not substitute for in-text attribution.
using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from your instructor.
units.policy: Cheating includes using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from the instructor.

units.anchor: using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results.
units.policy: Fabrication includes using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results.

units.anchor: faculty should follow the formal reporting process outlined in
units.policy: When a situation constitutes a Code of Student Conduct violation and AI-related academic misconduct, faculty should follow the formal reporting process in the Academic Integrity resources.

units.anchor: AI detection tools are not reliable indicators of AI use
units.policy: AI detection tools are not reliable indicators of AI use.

units.anchor: cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case
units.policy: AI detection results cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case.

units.anchor: can lead to biases in determination of culpability
units.policy: AI detection tools have been shown to produce inaccurate results and can lead to biases in determination of culpability.

units.anchor: A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove
units.policy: A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove a student used AI on an assignment.

units.anchor: Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended
units.policy: Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended and Approved, as doing so may violate institutional data privacy requirements.

units.anchor: Code similarity tools such as MOSS and JPlag occupy different evidentiary ground.
legitimate evidence of potential misconduct and may be submitted as part of a case
units.policy: A MOSS flag is not proof of AI use specifically, but it is legitimate evidence of potential misconduct and may be submitted as part of a case.

units.anchor: Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings.
faculty should rely on the behavioral evidence described below
units.policy: For ECE and other non-software courses where code similarity tools do not apply, faculty should rely on behavioral evidence.

units.anchor: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence
units.policy: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence such as style inconsistent with prior submissions, responses not addressing the prompt, fabricated facts or references, inconsistent word counts, or similarity to AI output when the prompt is entered into a model.

units.anchor: These categories apply across work products: text, code, simulations, circuit designs, lab reports
units.policy: The AI use categories apply across work products: text, code, simulations, circuit designs, lab reports, and other outputs.

units.anchor: faculty should interpret and apply them in the context of their discipline
units.policy: For non-software courses, faculty should interpret and apply the AI use categories in the context of their discipline.

units.anchor: using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material.
units.policy: The Clarification category is using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material.

units.anchor: brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches.
units.policy: The Idea generation category is brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches.

units.anchor: condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points.
units.policy: The Summarization category is condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points.

units.anchor: using AI to translate assignment prompts, source materials, or your own drafted text
units.policy: The Translation category is using AI to translate assignment prompts, source materials, or one's own drafted text into another language.

units.anchor: does not include submitting AI-translated text as original work without disclosure.
units.policy: The Translation category does not include submitting AI-translated text as original work without disclosure.

units.anchor: checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity within your own drafted text
units.policy: The Editing, proofreading, and formatting category is checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity within one's own drafted text, creating citations, tables and formatted documents, and converting material into alternate formats or plain language.

units.anchor: does not include rewriting full paragraphs.
units.policy: The Editing, proofreading, and formatting category does not include rewriting full paragraphs.

units.anchor: debugging code you wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept, or generating sample code
units.policy: The Coding assistance category is debugging code one wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept, or generating sample code strictly for learning purposes, for software code and hardware description and specification languages.

units.anchor: substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code you authored.
units.policy: The Rewriting or refactoring category is substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code one authored.

units.anchor: using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset
units.policy: The Analyzing data category is using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset, or to set up, run, or interpret simulation and modeling outputs.

units.anchor: this is the highest-stakes category and is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor
units.policy: Using AI to produce the primary work submitted for an assignment (text, code, graphics, audio, or other media) is the highest-stakes category and is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor.

units.anchor: unless the generated output is itself the object of analysis rather than the submitted work
units.policy: AI-generated work product is allowed when the generated output is itself the object of analysis rather than the submitted work product.

units.anchor: These tiers indicate when AI use in research should be disclosed
units.policy: Appendix B tiers indicate when AI use in research should be disclosed, absent stricter venue, funder, or IRB rules.

units.anchor: Where this table and venue rules differ, venue rules govern.
Disclosure is mandatory
units.policy: Research disclosure is mandatory when using AI to formulate questions or hypotheses or design experiments, draft or significantly revise text, translate the paper, collect, analyze, interpret, or visualize data, extract literature-review data, or generate synthetic data, images, or figures.

units.anchor: Disclosure is optional
units.policy: Research disclosure is optional when using AI to find or verify references, find examples, brainstorm organization or titles, or give feedback on one's own existing ideas, text, or code.

units.anchor: Disclosure is unnecessary
units.policy: Research disclosure is unnecessary when using AI to check grammar, spelling, punctuation, or formatting, search for sources, suggest clarifying words, autocomplete or act as a non-generating component, or act as a digital assistant.

units.anchor: do not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools for review assistance
units.policy: When reviewing manuscripts or grant proposals, reviewers must not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools, because doing so breaches the confidentiality of unpublished work.

units.anchor: Both NSF and NIH prohibit GenAI use in its peer review process.

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), graduate programs (ECE, CS, AI)
documents.title: EECS Graduate Handbook 2025-2026, Section 2.21 Guidelines for AI writing assistance and proper citation and attribution
documents.summary: Section 2.21 of the EECS Graduate Handbook (the only AI content in the handbook) limits graduate students' AI use to polishing and grammar-correcting writing they have already created, and bars using AI to create new content or research. It frames the rule around plagiarism, recommends Draft Coach similarity checks especially when AI was involved, explains self-plagiarism under copyright transfer, and requires due diligence for documents submitted to examination committees.

units.anchor: acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance if a student uses them
units.policy: Students may use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance to polish and correct the grammar of content they have already created.

units.anchor: may use AI tools to improve the writing and organization of that content created
units.policy: Students may use AI tools to improve the writing and organization of content they created, with the AI tool just polishing the final 10%.

units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research.
cannot ask ChatGPT to create an analysis or summary and then claim that text
units.policy: A student cannot ask ChatGPT to create an analysis or summary and then claim that text is their own writing.

units.anchor: ensure students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues
units.policy: The key requirement is that students do their own unique work and avoid plagiarism issues.

units.anchor: Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences.
Many careers have been ended by instances of plagiarism.
they may create content that is effectively copied from another author
units.policy: Because AI tools draw from existing writing, they may create content that is effectively copied from another author.

units.anchor: it is recommended that students use Draft Coach
units.policy: Students are recommended to use Draft Coach to check their work for similarity with other works, especially if an AI tool has been involved.

units.anchor: especially important for conference and journal publications, as submissions are run through plagiarism checkers
units.policy: Similarity checking is especially important for conference and journal publications, as submissions are run through plagiarism checkers.

units.anchor: they can get flagged by a plagiarism checker, even though those are their own words
units.policy: Because publishers generally acquire ownership of published content, students who reuse their own published text can be flagged for self-plagiarism even though the words are their own.

units.anchor: students perform due diligence, as described above or with equivalent mechanisms, for all documents
units.policy: The School requires students to perform due diligence (similarity checking as described, or equivalent mechanisms) for all documents submitted to their examination committees.

units.anchor: check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP.
units.policy: Students with further questions about proper policy, attribution, or academic integrity should check with their major advisor and/or the AHGP.

new_types.name: Define AI and its scope
new_types.definition: Definitions of AI, generative AI, AI tools or agentic systems that set what the policy covers (scope of 'AI use').

new_types.name: Govern AI use in research
new_types.definition: Rules for AI use in research and scholarship (theses, dissertations, manuscripts, grant proposals, peer review): advisor or committee norms, deference to venue, funder, sponsor or IRB rules, and research-specific obligations.

new_types.name: Provide faculty AI development and support
new_types.definition: The institution offers or recommends faculty training, workshops, consultations, communities of practice, or hands-on exploration of AI tools to help instructors set AI policy and teach with AI.

notes: Coder B. Course layer inaccessible per collect file, so no course documents. The syllabus-policy page is mostly non-AI syllabus requirements; only the AI usage element and its revision entry were coded. In the EECS graduate handbook only Section 2.21 is AI policy; the rest was read and contains no AI provisions. CTL guidance repeats the Syllabus Minimum Requirements AI clause; it was coded again in each document that states it, as each document is coded on its own. Template slots in CTL tier text (e.g., '[insert examples]') were coded only where the template itself states a rule. Appendix B disclosure tiers in the EECS guidance were coded as one unit per tier with the listed examples in the policy text.
